questions.stem: In the maturity stage of the business life cycle, a business typically experiences:
options: high start-up costs and no established customers
slowing sales growth and strong competition for market share
rapid sales growth as it first finds a loyal customer base
falling sales as its products become obsolete
questions.explanation: In maturity the business is established, but sales growth levels off and rivals compete hard for the same customers. Rapid growth describes the growth stage, and falling sales describe the post-maturity decline outcome.

questions.stem: A Toowoomba stockfeed maker has held 30% of its regional market for eight years. Sales are flat and two rivals have cut prices. Which challenge of the maturity stage does this best show?
options: raising enough seed capital to develop a first product
finding a first group of customers for an untested idea
managing the rapid hiring needed for fast sales growth
keeping market share in a saturated, competitive market
questions.explanation: Flat sales and price-cutting rivals in a market the business already dominates are typical of maturity. Raising seed capital and finding first customers are challenges of the seed and start-up stages.

questions.stem: Why might a mature business consider expanding into global markets?
options: global expansion guarantees lower costs than trading domestically
operating overseas removes exposure to competition from rivals
its domestic market is saturated, so growth must come from new customers
global markets remove any need to adapt its products to local conditions
questions.explanation: When the home market offers little more growth, new overseas customers can lift sales. Global expansion brings its own competition, costs and need to adapt, so none of the other claims hold.

questions.stem: Compared with a domestic market, a global market involves:
options: trading across national borders, with exposure to exchange rates
selling only within Australia under a single set of national laws
selling only to customers in the business's home state
trading only with businesses rather than with consumers
questions.explanation: A global market crosses national borders, so a business faces foreign currencies, laws and cultures. Selling within Australia under national law describes the domestic market.

questions.stem: A Cairns tourism business that earns most of its revenue from visitors from overseas is most directly exposed to:
options: changes in the Queensland liquor licensing fees
changes in the price of local council parking permits
changes in the number of Year 12 school leavers
changes in the exchange rate of the Australian dollar
questions.explanation: A stronger Australian dollar makes Australian holidays dearer for overseas visitors, so exchange rates directly affect its demand. The other factors are local and would have far smaller effects on overseas visitors.

questions.stem: A Brisbane coffee roaster buys a chain of cafes that sells its coffee to the public. This is:
options: horizontal growth, buying a business at the same stage
niche marketing, targeting a narrow group of customers
a licensing agreement for its brand in a new market
vertical growth, moving forward in the supply chain
questions.explanation: Buying the businesses that sell its product to consumers moves the roaster forward along its own supply chain, which is vertical growth. Horizontal growth would mean buying another coffee roaster.

questions.stem: A Mackay hardware chain buys a rival hardware chain in Rockhampton. Which expansion strategy is this?
options: backward vertical growth
forward vertical growth
a strategic alliance
horizontal growth
questions.explanation: Buying a business at the same stage of production in the same industry is horizontal growth. Vertical growth would involve buying a supplier (backward) or a distributor or retailer (forward).

questions.stem: A Bundaberg rum distiller buys the sugar mill that supplies its molasses. Which is the main advantage of this strategy?
options: a much larger share of the retail market for spirits in Australia
access to new overseas customers without any added risk
lower exposure to changes in consumer tastes for rum
more control over the supply, quality and cost of a key input
questions.explanation: Owning its supplier is backward vertical growth, giving the distiller control over its key input. It does not directly increase retail market share or reduce exposure to changing tastes.

questions.stem: A Gold Coast surfboard maker stops competing in the mass market and makes high-priced custom boards for professional surfers. Which strategy is this?
options: horizontal growth
mass marketing
joint venture
niche market
questions.explanation: Focusing on a small, specialised segment with particular needs is a niche market strategy. Mass marketing aims at the whole market, which is what the business is moving away from.

questions.stem: A mature Queensland food company spends heavily on research and development to create a new range of plant-based snacks for overseas markets. How does this support expansion?
options: research and development lowers its costs immediately in every year
innovation removes the need for any market research overseas
new products guarantee a larger share of the domestic market
innovation creates new products that open new markets and growth
questions.explanation: Research and development and innovation let a mature business offer something new, which can open new markets when existing products have stopped growing. It is costly in the short term, and new products still need research and carry no guarantee.

questions.stem: Under a licensing agreement for entering a global market, a business:
options: sets up and fully owns a new factory and sales office in that country
shares ownership of a new business with an overseas partner
sells its goods through an overseas agent paid by commission
lets an overseas firm use its brand or technology in return for royalties
questions.explanation: Licensing gives an overseas firm the right to use intellectual property, such as a brand, recipe or technology, in exchange for royalties. A fully owned overseas operation is a subsidiary, and shared ownership is a joint venture.

questions.stem: A Townsville maker of water filters wants to start selling in Indonesia with little investment and little knowledge of the local market. Which mode of entry best suits it?
options: using an international agent or distributor in Indonesia
building its own manufacturing subsidiary in Indonesia
buying an Indonesian water filter company outright
forming a joint venture to build a new Indonesian factory
questions.explanation: An agent or distributor already knows the local market and needs little investment, which suits a business testing a new market. Subsidiaries, acquisitions and joint ventures all require large commitments of money and management time.

questions.stem: An Australian wine company and a Japanese retailer agree to promote each other's products and share marketing costs, but each remains a separate business with no new company formed. This is:
options: a strategic alliance
a joint venture
an overseas sales subsidiary
a licensing agreement
questions.explanation: A strategic alliance is a cooperative agreement in which the businesses stay independent and no new entity is created. A joint venture creates a new business that the partners jointly own.

questions.stem: A Queensland mining services firm and a Vietnamese company each own 50% of a new company set up to operate in Vietnam. Which is a key risk of this mode of entry?
options: disagreements between partners over control, goals and profits
no access to local knowledge or contacts in Vietnam
the Queensland firm must carry the whole investment by itself
the new company cannot employ any local Vietnamese staff
questions.explanation: In a joint venture the partners share ownership and decisions, so conflicts over control and profit-sharing are a common risk. The main advantages are shared investment and the local partner's knowledge, which the distractors reverse.

questions.stem: A business ranks four modes of entry by the control it keeps over its overseas operations, from most to least. Which ranking is correct?
options: joint venture, exporting through an agent, wholly owned subsidiary, licensing
wholly owned subsidiary, joint venture, licensing, exporting through an agent
licensing, wholly owned subsidiary, exporting through an agent, joint venture
exporting through an agent, licensing, joint venture, wholly owned subsidiary
questions.explanation: A wholly owned subsidiary gives full control, a joint venture shares control, and licensing and agents hand most day-to-day control to another firm. Control generally rises with investment and risk, so the subsidiary sits at the top.

questions.stem: A SWOT analysis of entering China through a wholly owned sales subsidiary lists 'full control of brand and pricing' and 'high set-up cost and no local partner'. These two points are, in order:
options: a weakness and an opportunity in the market
a strength and a weakness of the mode of entry
an opportunity and a threat in the market
a threat and a strength of the mode of entry
questions.explanation: Both points describe internal features of the chosen mode, so they are a strength and a weakness. Opportunities and threats are external factors, such as Chinese demand or new regulations.

questions.stem: An initial public offering (IPO) is when a company:
options: borrows a large sum from a bank secured against its property
sells a share of the business privately to a large investment fund
receives a government grant to help it start exporting
first sells its shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange
questions.explanation: An IPO is a company's first offer of shares to the public, which lets it raise large amounts of equity and list on an exchange. Selling a stake privately to a fund is private equity finance.

questions.stem: A growing private company sells a 40% stake to an investment firm that also places two experienced directors on its board. This source of finance is:
options: a debenture issue
a government grant
private equity
an initial public offering
questions.explanation: Private equity is investment by funds or firms in companies not listed on a stock exchange, often with active involvement in management. An IPO sells shares to the public, and a debenture is a form of debt.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of financing global expansion through an initial public offering rather than a bank loan?
options: the company's assets must be pledged as security for the funds
the original owners give up some ownership and must meet listing rules
the company must make fixed interest payments whatever its profit is
the money must be repaid in full by a set date to the lender
questions.explanation: An IPO is equity finance, so owners dilute their ownership and the company takes on public reporting and listing obligations. Fixed interest, repayment dates and security are features of debt finance such as a bank loan.

questions.stem: A mature company keeps most of its profits rather than paying them to shareholders as dividends, to fund an overseas warehouse. What is a likely effect?
options: expansion is funded without new debt, but shareholders receive less income
the company's debt rises, increasing its interest costs in every year
the company must issue new shares and dilute existing ownership
shareholders receive higher dividends now and lower ones later
questions.explanation: Retaining profits is internal equity finance, so it adds no debt or new shares, but shareholders get lower dividends now. The other options describe debt finance, a share issue, or the reverse of the decision.

questions.stem: A Queensland exporter applies for an Australian Government grant to help pay for promoting its products overseas. A key advantage of this finance is that it:
options: replaces the need for any other source of finance
usually does not have to be repaid and carries no interest
gives the government a share of the exporter's future profits
can be obtained quickly with no conditions or reporting
questions.explanation: Grants are generally not repaid and carry no interest, though they come with eligibility rules and reporting requirements. Governments do not take a share of profits through a grant.

questions.stem: Which activity belongs to the development stage of the employment cycle?
options: inducting a new employee in their first week of work
training employees and building their skills for future roles
advertising vacancies and interviewing the job applicants who apply
processing an employee's resignation and final pay
questions.explanation: Development covers training, professional development and performance management that build employees' skills. Advertising and interviewing belong to acquisition, and resignation to separation.

questions.stem: A Sunshine Coast resort reviews its pay rates, offers flexible rosters and runs wellbeing programs to keep good staff. Which stage of the employment cycle is this?
options: separation
induction
maintenance
acquisition
questions.explanation: Maintenance is about keeping employees satisfied and productive through rewards, conditions and wellbeing. Acquisition is recruiting and selecting, and separation is when employees leave.

questions.stem: In a power interest grid, stakeholders with high power and high interest should be:
options: kept satisfied but not fully engaged
kept informed of major decisions
monitored with minimal effort
managed closely as key players
questions.explanation: Stakeholders with both high power and high interest can strongly affect the outcome and care about it, so they must be closely managed. Keeping satisfied suits high power but low interest stakeholders.

questions.stem: A company planning to list on the stock exchange places the Australian Securities and Investments Commission in the high power, low interest quadrant of its power interest grid. The company should:
options: manage it closely by consulting it on every business decision
keep it informed through regular customer newsletters
monitor it with minimal effort as it has little influence
keep the regulator satisfied by meeting all its requirements
questions.explanation: A regulator has great power over a listing but little interest in day-to-day decisions, so the company keeps it satisfied by complying fully. Close management is for high-power, high-interest key players.

questions.stem: A business plans to fund an overseas plant with a large bank loan. Its power interest grid shows local residents near its Australian factory as low power, high interest, and the bank as high power, high interest. Which conclusion follows?
options: treat both groups equally as they have the same level of interest
work closely with the bank and keep residents informed of the plans
work closely with residents and only monitor the bank's views
keep the bank satisfied and give residents no information at all
questions.explanation: The lender has high power and high interest, so it must be managed closely; residents are interested but have little power, so they should be kept informed. Ignoring residents risks reputation damage, and treating both the same ignores their different power.

questions.stem: Risk management during expansion involves:
options: avoiding every risk by not entering any new market at all
transferring every possible risk to customers through higher prices
responding to problems only after they have occurred
identifying, assessing and planning responses to possible risks
questions.explanation: Risk management identifies what could go wrong, assesses its likelihood and impact, and plans how to reduce or respond to it. Avoiding all risk would prevent expansion, and waiting until problems occur is reactive, not managed.

questions.stem: Before entering the Indonesian market, a Brisbane company takes out insurance against political unrest and arranges currency hedging. These actions are best described as:
options: an employer of choice strategy to attract skilled staff
horizontal growth through buying an overseas competitor
risk management that reduces the impact of external threats
a power interest grid analysis of the company's stakeholders
questions.explanation: Insurance and hedging reduce the financial impact of external risks such as unrest and currency movements, which is risk management. They have nothing to do with stakeholder mapping, staffing or buying rivals.

questions.stem: How is risk management related to strategic planning in a competitive market?
options: strategic plans set the goals, and risk management protects their achievement
risk management replaces the need for any objectives and strategies
strategic planning deals with risks only after expansion begins
risk management is only needed by businesses in the seed stage
questions.explanation: Strategic planning sets the direction and objectives, while risk management identifies threats to them and plans responses, so the two work together. Risk management supports planning rather than replacing it, and it matters at every stage.

questions.stem: Fiedler's contingency model proposes that a leader's effectiveness depends on:
options: the number of employees the leader is personally responsible for supervising
the leader's ability to change their style quickly for each task
the match between the leader's style and the favourableness of the situation
the leader using the same participative style in every situation
questions.explanation: Fiedler argued that leadership style is relatively fixed, so effectiveness depends on matching the leader to a situation that suits that style. The idea that leaders flexibly change style is closer to situational leadership.

questions.stem: Under Fiedler's contingency model, which three factors determine how favourable a situation is for the leader?
options: leader-member relations, task structure and position power
pay levels, working hours and the size of the business
employee skills, product quality and level of competition
the leader's age, experience and formal qualifications
questions.explanation: Fiedler measured situational favourableness by leader-member relations, how structured the task is, and the leader's formal position power. The other lists are not part of his model.

questions.stem: Under Fiedler's model, a task-oriented manager is struggling in a moderately favourable situation leading a new overseas project. Which response is most consistent with the model?
options: remove all structure from the task to give the team freedom
change the situation or appoint a leader whose style suits it
train the manager to switch to a relationship style overnight
leave the situation unchanged, as style has no effect on results
questions.explanation: Fiedler saw style as fixed, so the model suggests changing the situation or matching a different leader to it. Relationship-oriented leaders are predicted to do best in moderately favourable situations.

questions.stem: An intrapreneur is:
options: an owner who starts a new business by taking on all the personal risk
an outside consultant hired to review a business's finances
a manager who uses only rules and procedures to direct staff
an employee who develops innovative ideas within an existing business
questions.explanation: An intrapreneur acts like an entrepreneur but inside an existing organisation, using its resources to develop new ideas. An owner who starts a new business is an entrepreneur.

questions.stem: A Brisbane bank lets staff spend part of each week developing new app features, and one team's idea becomes a new product. Why does this help the bank in a competitive market?
options: it guarantees the bank will have lower costs than all its rivals
it means the bank no longer needs to recruit any skilled staff
it encourages intrapreneurs to create innovations that differentiate the bank
it removes any need for the bank to research its customers' changing needs
questions.explanation: Supporting intrapreneurs generates new ideas internally, helping a mature business stay ahead of competitors. It does not guarantee lower costs or replace customer research and recruitment.

questions.stem: An employer of choice is a business that:
options: chooses its employees only from people already known to the owner
is legally required to employ staff from a government list
pays only the minimum wage to keep its labour costs low
people want to work for because of its pay, conditions and culture
questions.explanation: An employer of choice attracts and keeps talented staff because of its reputation for good rewards, conditions, development and culture. Paying only the minimum would make that reputation hard to build.

questions.stem: Why are employer of choice strategies especially important for a business in the maturity stage of a competitive market?
options: keeping skilled, motivated staff helps it compete when products are similar
mature businesses no longer need to train or develop their staff
they allow a mature business to stop competing on its product quality
staff in mature businesses are not affected by pay or conditions
questions.explanation: In a mature market, rivals' products are often similar, so skilled and committed staff can be a key source of competitive advantage. Mature businesses still need to train staff and compete on quality.

questions.stem: A mining services company with many overseas projects recruits staff from a wide range of cultures, ages and backgrounds. How does this support its human resources strategic plan?
options: diverse teams never experience conflict or communication problems
diverse staff bring local knowledge, languages and ideas for new markets
a diverse workforce removes the need for any induction or training
it means the company no longer has to follow anti-discrimination law
questions.explanation: A diverse workforce can provide cultural understanding, language skills and a wider range of ideas, which helps a business expanding overseas. Diverse teams still need induction and inclusive management, and discrimination law always applies.

questions.stem: Staff turnover at a Rockhampton engineering firm is high. Exit interviews show staff were happy with pay and conditions but felt they had no recognition or chance to advance. Using Herzberg's two-factor theory, which strategy would best improve retention?
options: cut pay and conditions, as they have no link to staff satisfaction
improve the canteen and car park, as these are the key motivators
add motivators such as recognition, responsibility and promotion paths
raise pay further, as hygiene factors are the main source of motivation
questions.explanation: Herzberg found that hygiene factors such as pay and conditions prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate, while recognition, responsibility and advancement do. Since hygiene factors are already met, adding motivators should improve retention.

questions.stem: A company is entering several Asian markets at once and must persuade staff to embrace a bold new direction. Which leadership style best suits this expansion strategy?
options: bureaucratic, insisting that staff follow existing rules exactly
laissez-faire, leaving each team to decide whether to take part
transactional, relying only on rewards for staff meeting current targets
transformational, inspiring staff with a vision of the company's future
questions.explanation: Major expansion requires staff to accept change and commit to a new vision, which transformational leadership is built to achieve. Bureaucratic and transactional styles focus on existing rules and targets, which suits stable rather than changing situations.
